There was plenty of cold water to end their feast with. After a while Becky suggested that they start moving again. Tom said nothing for a moment. Then he asked:

“Becky, can you stand it if I tell you something?”

Becky turned pale, but she thought she could.

“Well, Becky, we have to stay here, where we have water to drink. That little piece is our last candle!”

Becky burst into tears and sobs. Tom tried his best to comfort her, but it did little good. At last she said:

“Tom!”

“Yes, Becky?”

“They’ll miss us and come looking for us!”

“Yes, they will! Of course they will!”

“Maybe they’re looking for us right now, Tom.”

“Well, I suppose they might be. I hope so.”

“When would they miss us, Tom?”

“When they get back to the boat, I suppose.”

“Tom, it might be dark by then—would they notice we weren’t there?”

“I don’t know. But your mother would miss you as soon as everyone got home.”

The frightened look on Becky’s face made Tom realize his mistake. Becky was not supposed to go home that night! The children fell silent, thinking. A moment later Becky began crying again, and Tom knew she had thought of the same thing he had: Sunday morning might be half over before Mrs. Thatcher learned that Becky was not at Mrs. Harper’s.

The children stared at their scrap of candle as it slowly, mercilessly melted away. At last only half an inch of wick remained. They watched its weak flame rise and sink, climb the thin trail of smoke, hang at the top for a moment, and then—the horror of complete darkness surrounded them!

Neither could tell how much later it was when Becky slowly became aware that she was crying in Tom’s arms. They knew only that, after what seemed an immense stretch of time, they both woke from a deep, exhausted sleep and faced their misery again. Tom said it might be Sunday now—perhaps even Monday. He tried to get Becky to talk, but she was too weighed down by sorrow. She had lost all hope. Tom said people must have missed them long ago and were surely searching. He would shout, and perhaps someone would come. He tried, but the distant echoes sounded so dreadful in the darkness that he did not try again.

The hours slipped away, and hunger began to torment the trapped children once more. Some of Tom’s half of the cake remained. They split it and ate it, but afterward they seemed hungrier than ever.

In fairness to the young lady, she did not state outright that she would refuse. She merely expressed a strong and heartfelt wish to be “blessed” if she agreed: a courteous, delicate way of avoiding the request, which shows that she possessed the natural good manners that shrink from hurting another person with a blunt and unmistakable refusal.

The Jew’s face fell. He turned from this young lady, dressed brightly, even splendidly, in a red gown, green boots, and yellow curling papers, to the other woman.

“Nancy, my dear,” said the Jew soothingly, “what do you say?”

“That it won’t work, so there’s no use trying it, Fagin,” Nancy replied.

“What do you mean by that?” Mr. Sikes asked, looking up sullenly.

“Exactly what I say, Bill,” the lady answered calmly.

“Why, you’re just the person for it,” Mr. Sikes argued. “Nobody around here knows anything about you.”

“And since I don’t want them to,” Nancy replied with the same composure, “my answer is rather more no than yes, Bill.”

“She’ll go, Fagin,” Sikes said.

“No, she won’t, Fagin,” Nancy said.

“Yes, she will, Fagin,” Sikes said.

And Mr. Sikes was right. Through a succession of threats, promises, and bribes, the lady was eventually persuaded to carry out the errand. Her hesitation did not, in fact, arise from the same concerns as her agreeable friend’s. Having recently moved to the neighborhood of Field Lane from the distant but respectable suburb of Ratcliffe, she did not share the same fear of being recognized by any of her many acquaintances.

So, with a clean white apron tied over her dress and her curling papers tucked beneath a straw bonnet—both garments supplied from the Jew’s inexhaustible stock—Miss Nancy prepared to set out on her errand.

“Wait a minute, my dear,” said the Jew, bringing out a small covered basket. “Carry this in one hand. It looks more respectable, my dear.”

“Give her a door key to carry in the other, Fagin,” Sikes said. “It makes it look real and genuine.”

“Yes, yes, my dear, so it does,” said the Jew, hanging a large front-door key on the forefinger of the young lady’s right hand. “There, very good! Very good indeed, my dear!” he said, rubbing his hands.

“Oh, my brother! My poor, dear, sweet, innocent little brother!” Nancy cried, bursting into tears and twisting the little basket and the front-door key in an agony of distress. “What has happened to him? Where have they taken him? Oh, please have pity and tell me what they’ve done with the dear boy, gentlemen. Please, gentlemen, if you would be so kind, gentlemen!”

To see a star clearly, glance at it from the side, letting its light fall on the outer parts of the retina, which respond better to faint light than the inner parts. This gives you the clearest sense of its brightness. The more directly you look at it, the dimmer it becomes. More rays of light actually enter the eye when you look straight at it, but a sideways glance allows you to perceive it more sensitively. Thinking too deeply can confuse and weaken our thoughts. Even Venus can be made to disappear from the sky if we stare at her too steadily, too intently, or too directly.

“As for these murders, let us investigate a little ourselves before forming an opinion about them. The inquiry will give us some amusement”—I thought that a strange word to use, but said nothing—“and besides, Le Bon once did me a favor that I have not forgotten. We will go and look at the place ourselves. I know G——, the chief of police, and should have no trouble getting the permission we need.”

Permission was granted, and we went straight to the Rue Morgue. This is one of the wretched streets between the Rue Richelieu and the Rue St. Roch. We arrived late in the afternoon, since the neighborhood was far from the one where we lived. The house was easy to find. Across the street, many people were still staring up at its closed shutters with idle curiosity. It was an ordinary Paris house with a gateway. On one side stood a small glass-fronted booth with a sliding window panel, showing that this was the caretaker’s room. Before entering, we walked farther up the street, turned into an alley, and turned again to pass behind the building. All the while, Dupin examined the house and the entire neighborhood with such close attention to detail that I could not imagine what purpose it served.

We went back the way we had come and returned to the front of the house. We rang the bell, showed our papers, and were let in by the officers in charge. We climbed the stairs to the room where Mademoiselle L’Espanaye’s body had been found and where both victims still lay. As was usual, the room’s disorder had been left untouched. I saw nothing beyond what the “Gazette des Tribunaux” had reported. Dupin examined everything closely, including the victims’ bodies. We then visited the other rooms and the yard, with a police officer accompanying us the whole time.
